exp: 4, then 3, then 2. numbers keeps all four elements including the duplicate 20 (Lists allow duplicates). unique collapses the two 20s into one, giving 3 distinct values. countByValue counts occurrences per value, and 20 appears twice in numbers, so its count is 2.
expl: numbers.size() is 4 because a List's contract never removes or rejects duplicates -- all four values passed to List.of(...) are present exactly as given. unique.size() is 3 because constructing a HashSet from numbers applies a Set's no-duplicates guarantee during construction, collapsing the two separate 20 entries down into a single element -- leaving 10, 20, and 30, three distinct values. countByValue.get(20) is 2 because the loop increments a running count for each value it encounters, using getOrDefault(n, 0) to start counting from 0 for a value seen for the first time; since 20 appears twice in numbers, its count is incremented twice, landing at 2.

Coordinate overrides equals() to compare x and y by content, but never overrides hashCode(), so it still inherits Object's default, identity-based hashCode() -- meaning two Coordinate objects with identical x and y values, but different memory addresses, produce different hash codes. HashMap's containsKey() first computes the hash code of the Coordinate being looked up to find which bucket to search, and only then uses equals() to check candidates within that bucket -- if the new Coordinate(1, 1) hashes to a different bucket than the one actually holding the stored entry, equals() never even gets a chance to run, and containsKey() reports false despite the two objects clearly being .equals(). Adding a hashCode() override based on the same fields equals() uses (via Objects.hash(x, y)) guarantees that any two Coordinates that are .equals() also hash identically, letting HashMap actually find the right bucket and then confirm the match.

exp: true, then AMY. namesPair and numbersPair are both run-time instances of the same erased class Pair, so their getClass() results are identical, regardless of the different type arguments used when constructing each one. namesPair.getFirst() returns "Amy", and .toUpperCase() on it gives "AMY".
expl: Pair<String> and Pair<Integer> are both, after erasure, simply instances of the one class Pair -- the type argument used at construction time (String or Integer) has no bearing on the object's actual run-time class, so namesPair.getClass() == numbersPair.getClass() is true, exactly analogous to List<String> and List<Integer> sharing ArrayList.class. Separately, namesPair.getFirst() returns the value stored in first for that specific instance, "Amy" -- and because namesPair was declared as Pair<String>, the compiler already knows getFirst()'s return type is specifically String for this call, inserting whatever cast is needed automatically, so calling .toUpperCase() directly on the result compiles and runs without any explicit cast being written, producing "AMY".

new T[capacity] is illegal because, after type erasure, T no longer exists as a real type at the point the array would actually be created -- the JVM needs a genuine, concrete element type to allocate an array (arrays track their element type at run time for array-store checks), and there's nothing left for T to be at that point. The standard, idiomatic workaround, used internally by real generic collection classes like ArrayList, is to back the class with a plain Object[] instead, which is always a legal, concrete array type to create. push() stores items into that Object[] without needing any cast (every T is already an Object). pop(), however, needs to hand back a T to its caller, and reading an Object out of items and treating it as a T requires an explicit cast, (T) items[--size] -- one the compiler cannot fully verify is safe at run time (since T is erased), which is exactly why it's paired with @SuppressWarnings("unchecked") to acknowledge that the class's own internal logic (only ever storing T values via push()) is what actually guarantees the cast's safety, not anything the compiler itself can check.

exp: [Kim:50, Lee:65, Jo:80] then [Jo:80, Kim:50, Lee:65]. The first sort uses compareTo(), ordering ascending by score. The second sort uses an explicit Comparator by name, completely replacing the score-based order with alphabetical order by name.
expl: Collections.sort(players) with no explicit Comparator falls back to each element's own compareTo(), which Player defines to compare by score ascending -- so the first printed list orders Kim(50), Lee(65), Jo(80) from lowest to highest score. The second sort call passes Comparator.comparing((Player p) -> p.name) explicitly, which entirely replaces the ordering used for this call -- it does not defer to or combine with compareTo() in any way. That Comparator extracts each Player's name and compares using String's natural alphabetical order, giving Jo, Kim, Lee alphabetically, so the second printed list is [Jo:80, Kim:50, Lee:65], completely unrelated to the score-based order from the line before it.

this.priceInCents - other.priceInCents computes the mathematical difference using ordinary int arithmetic, which has a fixed range -- if priceInCents holds values near Integer.MAX_VALUE and Integer.MIN_VALUE respectively (or close enough to those extremes), the true difference can exceed what an int can represent, and Java's int arithmetic silently wraps around (overflows) rather than throwing any error. That wraparound can flip the sign of the result entirely, making compareTo() report 'this is smaller' when it's actually larger, or vice versa -- which corrupts the sort for exactly those extreme-value pairs while appearing to work correctly for every ordinary-sized value, making the bug easy to miss in casual testing. Integer.compare(a, b) is implemented specifically to avoid this: it returns the correct sign for any two int values without ever performing a subtraction that could overflow, which is exactly why it -- along with Double.compare, Long.compare, and the other wrapper-class compare() methods -- is the idiomatic, safe choice inside any compareTo() or Comparator, rather than hand-rolled subtraction.

expl: For i = 0 and i = 1, neither if triggers, so both print normally. For i = 2, the continue statement runs, which skips only the println below it for this one iteration and jumps straight to the loop's update step (i++) and next condition check -- the loop itself keeps going. For i = 3, again neither if triggers, so it prints normally. For i = 4, the break statement runs, which terminates the loop immediately and completely -- its println never executes, and no further iterations happen at all (i = 5 is never reached, since the loop has already ended). The final output is therefore 0, 1, 3 -- three lines, with 2 skipped by continue and 4 (and anything beyond it) cut off entirely by break.

The condition i > 0 can only ever become false if i eventually reaches 0 or goes negative -- but the original code uses i++, which increments i further away from zero on every iteration, guaranteeing i > 0 stays true forever and the loop never terminates. Changing i++ to i--, so i counts down instead of up, means i decreases by one each pass (5, 4, 3, 2, 1), and once i reaches 0, the condition i > 0 finally evaluates to false and the loop ends -- printing exactly 5, 4, 3, 2, 1 in that order, matching the intended behavior.

expl: NumberFormatException extends IllegalArgumentException, which extends RuntimeException -- so it is a subtype of RuntimeException, not an unrelated type. expl: javac's entire job is to translate source text into a .class file; once that file exists, it's a self-contained artifact that no longer depends on the source that produced it. `java Calculator` tells the JVM to find a class named Calculator (via the classloader, which looks for Calculator.class in the classpath) and execute its bytecode starting at main -- it never reads or needs Calculator.java at all. normalized == "quit" compares object identity, not text content -- and normalized is built via new String(...), which explicitly creates a brand-new heap object rather than reusing anything from the string literal pool. Even when normalized's characters are exactly "quit", it is never the same object as the literal "quit" used on the right-hand side, so == is false essentially every time, regardless of the actual text. The fix, normalized.equals("quit"), compares character content instead of object identity, which is what 'does this string say quit' actually means. This bug is a direct, practical instance of the == vs .equals() trap: it happens to look like it might work in quick testing (if you'd used a literal instead of new String(...), the literal pool could accidentally make == appear to succeed), which is exactly what makes it dangerous in real code.

Inside it, super.describe() explicitly calls Vehicle's version, returning 'a vehicle', and Car's override appends that into 'a car, which is a vehicle', which is what ultimately gets printed.

Two separate bugs here. First, Square's constructor tries to assign width and height directly without ever calling a Rectangle constructor -- but every subclass constructor's first statement must be a call to a superclass constructor, and since Rectangle has no accessible no-argument constructor for Java to insert implicitly, this fails to compile with something like 'constructor Rectangle in class Rectangle cannot be applied to given types' or a missing-super error. The fix replaces the direct field assignments with super(side, side), letting Rectangle's own constructor do the actual initialization. Second, the method is written as Area() (capital A), which does not match Rectangle's area() (lowercase a) -- @Override specifically catches this: since there's no Rectangle method with that exact signature to override, the annotation itself makes this a compile error rather than silently letting Area() become an unrelated new method that never actually overrides anything. Renaming it to area() fixes the mismatch and makes @Override valid.

exp: EMAIL: URGENT: server down. sendUrgent (the interface default) calls send("URGENT: server down"), which dispatches to BaseNotifier's implementation, printing prefix ("EMAIL") followed by the message.
expl: n.sendUrgent("server down") runs Notifier's default method, since neither BaseNotifier nor EmailNotifier overrides it. That default builds the string "URGENT: server down" and calls send(...) with it -- and that call dispatches based on the real run-time type of n, which is an EmailNotifier. EmailNotifier itself has no send() of its own, but it inherits BaseNotifier's implementation, which prints prefix + ": " + message. prefix was set to "EMAIL" via EmailNotifier's constructor calling super("EMAIL"), so the final output is "EMAIL: URGENT: server down" -- a chain running from the interface's default, into the abstract class's concrete implementation, using state set up by the concrete subclass's constructor.

err:
Main.java:13: error: Contractor is not abstract and does not override abstract method calculatePay() in Payable
class Contractor extends Worker {
^
1 error
expl: Worker is allowed to implement Payable without providing calculatePay() itself, precisely because Worker is declared abstract -- an abstract class is permitted to leave inherited abstract methods (whether from an interface or from an abstract superclass) unimplemented, deferring the obligation to whichever subclass eventually becomes concrete. Contractor, however, is a plain, concrete class, and a concrete class is never allowed to leave any inherited abstract method unimplemented -- since Contractor extends Worker and never supplies calculatePay(), the compiler correctly rejects it with something like 'Contractor is not abstract and does not override abstract method calculatePay() in Payable'. The fix adds a real calculatePay() implementation to Contractor, computing pay from its own hourlyRate and hoursWorked fields, which finally satisfies the obligation Payable originally imposed and Worker deliberately left open.
